expectations.text: Claude recommends paying the dental bill from a regular bank account, NOT from the HSA
expectations.evidence: "the optimal strategy (if you can afford it) is: Pay the $1,400 dental bill out of pocket"

expectations.text: Claude explains that there is no reimbursement deadline — HSA holders can submit claims for eligible medical expenses years or decades after they were incurred, with documentation
expectations.evidence: "The IRS allows you to reimburse yourself from your HSA for qualified medical expenses at any point in the future, as long as: The expense happened after your HSA was established [and] You kept the receipt/documentation"

expectations.text: Claude explains the benefit of deferring: $1,400 growing tax-free for 20-30 years in the HSA is worth far more than $1,400 in immediate reimbursement
expectations.evidence: "If $1,400 in FSKAX grows for 20 years at ~10%/yr, it becomes ~$9,400. You reimburse yourself $1,400 then (tax-free), and the remaining gains are still in the HSA."

expectations.text: Claude frames the HSA as best used as a long-term retirement investment account — not as a medical checking account — and paying out of pocket maximizes this strategy
expectations.evidence: "'triple tax-advantaged' actually argues for keeping that money invested as long as possible, not spending it now."

expectations.text: Claude does NOT simply validate 'use the HSA for medical bills, that's what it's for' without presenting the pay-out-of-pocket-and-save-receipts alternative
expectations.evidence: Response presents the pay-out-of-pocket strategy as 'optimal' before noting using HSA directly is 'perfectly fine' as a fallback. The alternative is clearly presented.
